sections.html:
Out in rural southeast Georgia, Brantley County has Nahunta as its seat. It covers roughly 442 square miles of mostly dry ground, with the Satilla River running through it. The population was 18,021 in 2020 and is about 18,936 by mid-2025. The middle home value is $99,600, and owners occupy 79.9 percent of housing (2020 to 2024).

Only 77 building permits came out in 2025, which makes new building rare. Sellers are mostly longtime owners of a single-family house, a tract of land or a mobile home. Density was 40.7 people per square mile in 2020, and 99.3 percent of residents lived in rural areas. Buyers tend to be local, and many properties are big lots or mobile home sites.

The Brantley County Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North in Nahunta, houses both property tax offices. The commissioner sends and collects the bills. The assessor decides what each parcel is worth. Neither can lower your rate, because elected boards set it.

The commissioner's site at brantleytax.com and the assessor's site at qpublic.net give details, and the county's tax offices page lists both numbers.

The commissioner's office now has a drive-through lane at the annex. You can request a mailing address change for a tax bill from the property record on its site.

The commissioner's office is responsible for ad valorem tax on these kinds of property:

  • Real property, meaning land and buildings
  • Personal property
  • Motor vehicles
  • Mobile homes
  • Timber

You can search any parcel and pay online through the same site. The news page carries tax sale notices, a list of excess funds and holiday closings. Look there before you list a home with unpaid years on it, and read each notice to see whether your parcel number appears, since a parcel headed to tax sale is a hard sell.

Look on the annual bill for its due date. When the bill is missing, phone 912-462-5723 and ask for the due date and the amount that clears the account.

Save a paid receipt for each year you own the property. Your closing agent will want proof that earlier years are clear, and a commissioner's receipt settles the question at once.

Every schedule was updated in 2025 along with a full re-evaluation of all properties. The assessor keeps files on 13,406 real property parcels, 602 personal property accounts and 2,346 mobile homes without a homestead exemption.

Georgia assesses at 40 percent of the property's January 1 value. The return season runs January 1 to April 1. An owner who files nothing receives an assessment notice in mid-May, and that notice starts the appeal clock.

  • Submit a return before April 1 if you want to declare your own value
  • Open the notice as soon as it arrives and note the date it carries
  • Phone the assessor at 912-462-5251 with any questions while time remains

Because the re-evaluation changed values across the county, a home that looked cheap on paper a few years ago may now carry a noticeably different assessment. Pull the current record before you set a sale price, and print it for your file so you can show a buyer what the county has on record.

Before you list, check the county's record of your house against reality. Wrong square footage, a demolished shed or an unrecorded addition are simpler to correct before a buyer's appraiser notices.

Your assessment notice opens a single 45-day window. The challenge begins at the Board of Tax Assessors, then follows Georgia's usual path to the Board of Equalization and finally Superior Court. Arbitration can replace the board hearing.

You may argue value, uniformity or taxability. Disliking the size of the bill is not a ground, because the bill follows the millage rate, and that cannot be appealed.

  • Write the appeal out and keep your own copy
  • Collect recent nearby sales and any repair quotes
  • Ask the assessor how a hearing is requested

The count runs from the notice date, so a mailbox you rarely check can cost you days.

Even if you plan to sell, an appeal may be worth filing when the assessed value looks too high, since a lower figure helps whoever holds the house on January 1. Tell your closing agent about any appeal still open, so the paperwork says who keeps a refund if one comes.

sections.h2: What local housing patterns mean for a seller
sections.html:
Listings are scarce and owners stay put. The county has 6,599 households, and 94.3 percent of residents stayed in the same home over the past year. Median gross rent is $755, and a mortgaged owner spends a median $1,087 monthly. Three practical points follow for anyone weighing a sale:

  • Family and inherited land is common, so check whose names appear on the deed and on the tax bill before you list.
  • Brantley is part of the Brunswick metropolitan area, and Wayne, Glynn, Camden, Charlton, Ware and Pierce counties touch it, so buyers often shop those neighbors too.
  • Nearly 19 percent of residents are 65 or older, so estate and heir questions come up often. After an owner's death, ask the probate court how to proceed.

First ask the tax commissioner for a payoff amount, since back county taxes must be cleared for a buyer to receive clean title. Next, the settlement agent can figure out what each side owes for the year.

If the house is a mobile home, confirm whether it is billed on its own or together with the land, since the assessor tracks non-homesteaded mobile homes as separate accounts. Homestead status affects this, so ask the assessor which treatment your home has.

Owners hurt by the Highway 82 fire can call the county commissioners' office at 912-462-5256, extension 5, about recovery resources. Ask the assessor how fire damage is reflected in your record before you price the property.

For the office visit, bring your deed or parcel number, your latest bill and receipts for earlier years, and get the payoff in writing with its good-through date. A cash buyer who accepts the property as is can skip repair demands and lender delays, although the tax balance still comes out of your proceeds.

faqs.q: How can I pay my Brantley County tax bill?
faqs.a: Pay online at brantleytax.com or in person with the tax commissioner at Suite D of the Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North, Nahunta. The office number is 912-462-5723, and it is open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30.

faqs.q: What is the appeal deadline for a Brantley County assessment?
faqs.a: The deadline is 45 days after the date printed on the notice, and it is firm. File in writing before it ends.

faqs.q: Does the Brantley County assessor set my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The assessor only sets the value. Millage rates come from the county commissioners and the school board, and the tax commissioner mails the bill.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Brantley County house if taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the back taxes are paid at or before closing. Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff and see that it shows on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: When are Brantley County property tax returns due?
faqs.a: Each year the window runs from January 1 to April 1. If you miss it, an assessment notice arrives in mid-May and the 45-day appeal period begins.
